name: table-module
intent: Organise the domain logic of a table or view as one module with a single instance whose operations act on whole sets of rows, so table-shaped rules are written once against tabular record sets instead of being scattered over per-row objects or per-request procedures.
problem: The rules for a table are set-shaped - recalculating a column across all rows, validating an import batch, posting a period, aggregating or exporting a whole table - and the platform already speaks in tables and record sets (result sets, DataTables, grids, reports). A Domain Model would build one object per row and pay for identity, hydration and per-object behaviour the rules never use, while a Transaction Script repeats the same table-shaped logic in every use case that touches the table.
context: Data-centric enterprise applications with moderate, table-shaped logic: batch jobs, imports and reconciliation, reporting and export modules, and applications whose UI and data tooling is table-based (typed DataSets, data grids, report engines). It assumes that data access is already provided by a Table Data Gateway or equivalent, and that callers - typically a Service Layer - own the transaction boundary around the module's calls.
benefits: One owner per table: every rule about a table lives in one module, so there is exactly one place to read, change and test it.
Nothing is hydrated: rows stay records inside a record set, so there is no per-row object graph, no identity map and no lazy-loading machinery to build or debug.
Set-oriented by construction: rules the database can express as one statement stay one statement, which keeps round trips and memory low for bulk work (postings, recalculations, exports).
Fits table-shaped tooling: record sets go straight to grids, reports, CSV/Excel writers and import pipelines without an object-to-row translation layer.
Low ceremony for moderate logic: fewer classes than a Domain Model, and a new operation is one method on an existing module rather than a new collaboration of objects.
Keeps the data-access boundary visible: SQL stays in a gateway behind the module, so the module can be read and reasoned about as rules over rows.
tradeoffs: No per-row identity or behaviour: anything that must hold of one row as a unit (lifecycle, invariants, polymorphic row types) has no natural home and degrades into column flags and switches.
Schema coupling: one module per table binds the logic to the table's shape, so a schema or view change ripples directly into the module.
The module is a growth magnet: a busy table accumulates every rule, query and report, and the class turns into a god object unless it is split deliberately.
Transactions are external: without a Service Layer or unit of work, a rule spanning several tables can commit partially, and no module owns the consistency of the whole operation.
Testing wants the real schema: a hand-built record set is a poor fake, so tests usually run against an embedded database and pure unit isolation is harder than with a Domain Model.
Row-by-row use is a trap: the same module invites per-row calls, which become N+1 statements and abandon the set-oriented pass that justified the pattern.

participants.responsibility: The single instance holding the procedures that act on all rows of one table or view; it is the module's API and the only place that table's rules live.

The in-memory tabular data (DataTable, result list, Row/Seq[Row], array of row structs) that the module's operations accept and return; it carries rows plus column metadata and is not a graph of domain objects.
The usual collaborator that holds all SQL for one table and returns record sets to the module, keeping statements out of the rules and rules out of the SQL.
Calls the module's procedures, provides the transaction boundary for use cases spanning several modules, and does not manipulate the module's rows directly.

use_cases: Periodic batch posting: recompute balances or fees for every row in a period in one set-oriented pass.
Import and reconciliation: validate, normalise and promote a staging table before its rows become live data, reporting row-level errors as a batch.
Reporting and export modules that fetch a record set for a grid, report engine or CSV/Excel export, where tabular output is the goal.
Bulk recalculation after a rule change: apply a corrected formula to all existing rows of a table without loading them into a model.
Small-to-medium applications where each table has a handful of well-defined operations and no rich invariants spanning rows or tables.
Cleansing and reconciliation jobs over an operational table where the database should do the heavy lifting (aggregate, update ... where) and the application only orchestrates.
.NET ADO.NET typed DataSet / typed DataTable modules: the generated table is the record set, business methods operate over all its rows and it binds directly to grids and report controls.

Ruby on Rails set-oriented surface: an ActiveRecord::Relation scoped to one table applies table-wide rules via update_all/delete_all as a single SQL statement without instantiating row models, whose official documentation warns that validations and callbacks are skipped so the statement must carry the rule.

Django set-wide recalculation: QuerySet.update() and bulk_update() write whole filtered sets with direct SQL that bypasses per-row save(), used exactly where per-object persistence would mean one round trip per row.
avoid_when: The domain has rich invariants that must hold per entity or across an aggregate - use a Domain Model with Aggregate and a Data Mapper instead.
Each use case is a straight-line procedure over a few rows - a Transaction Script is simpler and honest.
Only access logic is needed, with no business rules - a Table Data Gateway alone is the right size and a module would be an empty layer.
The platform or team already maps rows to entities (JPA/Hibernate, EF Core, ActiveRecord) - use that mapping (Domain Model/Active Record) instead of building a parallel table API.
Rules must be polymorphic across row types (one column decides behaviour) - Type Object/Domain Model express that, a table module turns it into switches.
Concurrent in-place mutation of the same rows is the core requirement - a table module has no per-row locking strategy, so row-level state and optimistic locking must be designed explicitly.
anti_patterns: God table module: one class per table that accumulates every rule, report and query until the module is thousands of lines and no longer a coherent unit.
Pass-through module: a class that only forwards calls to the gateway with no rules of its own, adding a layer and no value.
Load-everything loops: pulling a whole table into memory and iterating in the host language for a rule a single UPDATE or aggregate could express.
Row-by-row module use inside a loop over rows, producing N+1 statements - the performance bug the pattern was supposed to prevent.
String-concatenated SQL inside the module instead of bound parameters, usually introduced when the module starts to add one filter at a time.
Direct row mutation by presentation code that bypasses the module, so the rules live in two places at once.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: rules in the Table Module, SQL in the Table Data Gateway, orchestration and transactions in a Service Layer.
Cohesion by data: group behaviour by the table whose rows it acts on - the organising principle of the pattern.
Single responsibility per module: one table or view owns one module, and that module owns only its table's rules.
Encapsulation: the module exposes set operations, never raw statements or connections.
Set-oriented thinking: prefer operations over collections of rows to operations over a single row, matching the database's execution model.
Explicit transaction boundaries: consistency is the caller's contract, and the module must not hide transaction decisions inside rules.
best_practices: Define the module API in terms of record sets and typed row structures, not object graphs; the signature is where the pattern becomes visible.
Keep one Table Data Gateway (or repository) behind the module and keep SQL text out of everything else.
Wrap multi-table use cases in a Service Layer that owns the transaction, with a unit of work when several modules take part.
Use the database for bulk work - UPDATE, INSERT ... SELECT, aggregate queries - and iterate rows only when the query language cannot express the rule.
Return typed rows (typed DataTable, generated record class, row struct) so column drift is caught by the compiler or by a single mapping point.
Test against an embedded database with the real schema and keep a few pure tests for rules over synthetic record sets.
Split the module once it stops fitting one coherent unit of behaviour: by use case, by concern, or by moving the object-shaped parts to a richer model.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2002) - Table Module (Domain Logic Patterns), with the companion patterns Record Set and Table Data Gateway.
